Living Well / Essay

When technology helps you notice more

Essay · 4 min read · Published October 9, 2026

On this page
  1. Begin with what caught your attention
  2. A bird, a name, and something to check
  3. The same idea, through an image
  4. An equally valid route without an app
  5. What would make the tool worth keeping?
  6. Let curiosity fit where you are
  7. One question to take with you

A screen can pull you away from your surroundings. It can also help you ask a better question about something already there. The distinction is what happens after you open it.

Begin with what caught your attention

Imagine noticing a bird outside a window. You do not know its name, but you have noticed a shape, a movement, or a repeated sound. That small uncertainty is enough to begin. You do not need to turn it into a hobby, make a public observation, or plan a special outing.

This is an illustrative situation, not a report of an outing Nolan has taken. The useful question is whether a tool helps you return to what you noticed with a little more understanding. A perfect identification is not the only worthwhile outcome. You might simply learn which features deserve a closer look.

A bird, a name, and something to check

Cornell Lab’s Merlin Bird ID offers bird-identification help in a free app. Its official guide explains email confirmation for continued use, regional coverage, and why a possible match may be missing or mistaken. Sound ID does not cover every region equally.

Use a proposed identification as a question to examine. Does the description fit what you actually observed? Which feature led to the suggestion? Do not quietly replace an uncertain detail with what the app expected. There is a difference between learning a likely name and knowing that an identification is correct.

Setup is part of the cost even when the app is free. Read the official access information before installing, and use the links supplied by the provider. The point is to support a moment of curiosity, not to create another account or collection unless you actually want one.

The same idea, through an image

Seek by iNaturalist offers image-based identification for plants and animals. It is free and basic use does not require registration. Its optional iNaturalist connection and posting features have a different data-sharing context, described in the Seek privacy information.

A suggested match can give you a place to start reading. It need not become a badge to collect. Pay attention to the thing itself before and after consulting the screen. You can also decline to photograph or upload anything: discovering a name and sharing an observation are separate choices.

Do not use an app’s guess to decide whether something is safe to eat, touch, or approach. Observe without disturbing wildlife or entering an unsafe place. An ordinary identification aid should remain separate from a consequential safety decision.

An equally valid route without an app

Notice one feature you can describe, such as a pattern, a sound, a location, or a way of moving. Keep the uncertainty in the description. Later, a field guide, a public information sign, or someone knowledgeable may help you investigate it. A brief paper note is enough if you need a reminder.

You may also choose not to identify it at all. Knowing the name of something can enrich an experience; it does not grant permission to have the experience. There is nothing wrong with noticing the changing light, an unfamiliar call, or a detail in a familiar room and leaving it there.

What would make the tool worth keeping?

Ask whether the interaction made you more available to your surroundings. Did you notice another detail? Did a question become clearer? Or did you spend the rest of the moment managing a list, correcting guesses, and thinking about what to capture next? These are questions for your own use, not validated measures of attention.

A tool is allowed to help occasionally. You do not have to build a routine around it or justify having installed it through repeated use. Equally, a device that supports access may remain important throughout an activity. Presence is not defined by how little technology someone uses.

Let curiosity fit where you are

This does not require walking, traveling, hearing a particular sound, or seeing a particular detail. Begin with what is accessible: a view from a seat, a recording you can explore, a texture you know is safe to touch, a description, or another person’s observation. Keep the devices and support you need.

The free-resource collection includes these two apps and a different kind of doorway, borrowing through Libby. They serve different interests. The shared editorial idea is simple: use technology for a purpose you can name, and let the experience be larger than the tool.

One optional practice

Choose one familiar setting and notice a detail you would normally pass over. Investigate it with a suitable source or leave the question open. This is an optional invitation, not a trial with results to report.

Keep any notes privately. Skip or adapt this exercise if it does not fit your circumstances.

One question to take with you

What did the tool help you notice that was still there after you put it away?
